newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami faces fight over cabinet posts.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami faces fight over cabinet posts.

text.p: New President Mohammad Khatami faces a stern political challenge next week when he tries to secure approval for his cabinet in Iran's conservative-dominated parlaiment.

Tehran political sources said on Saturday it was likely that Khatami would present a letter containing his choice of cabinet ministers to the parliament, or Majlis, soon after it reconvenes on Sunday.

The 270-member parliament, led by a conservative faction dedictated to supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, is expected to scrutinise kep positions such as the foreign, interior and culture ministries.
The final composition of the cabinet will be key to the tone and reforming character of the 54-year-old Shi'ite cleric's four-year term of office.
"Khamenei and his supporters are objecting to certain candidates...It looks unlikely that Khatami will be able to push through his appointments that quickly," said a diplomat.
Majlis members are expected to take a week to review the submitted letter.

Entrenched revolutionaries and conservative clerics were behind Khatami's fall from power in 1992 when they forced him to step down as culture minister, accusing him of not doing enough to stop Western cultural values taking root in the Islamic state.

Khatami, seen by his backers as a moderate able to breathe more social and economic freedom into the 18-year-old Islamic republic, needs a cabinet whose complexion is relatively moderate if he is to fulfil election promises, analysts said.
The cabinet is expected to contain at least one woman for the first time since the 1979 revolution which overthrew the U.S.-backed Shah, the English-language Iran news daily said.
Khatami was sworn in on Monday and has until August 18 to submit his cabinet which would consist of some 22 ministers. So far he has not made public his possible choices.

The fighting over possible cabinet appointments was reflected in fierce editorials in Iranian newspapers on Saturday, highlighting deep divisions between backers of Khatami and conservative elements in parliament and other state bodies run by the hardline clerical establishment.
"People have the right to ask what problems their supported president is facing in preparing and finalising his cabinet," Iran newspaper, which supports Khatami, said.

"People have wished your (conservatives) defeat in the elections and today you don't have the right to bully the executive officials of the country under the name of Majlis majority and tell him whom to choose for membership of his cabinet."

Khatami overwhelmingly beat Majlis speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri in the May election, scooping nearly 70 percent of the popular vote despite the establishment's implicit support of the more hardline Nateq-Nouri.
The leftist Islamist paper Salam, which strongly backed Khatami's run in May, urged the president to publicly tell his supporters the problems he faced in securing his own appointments.
Conservative newspapers have criticised Khatami's reformist and radical supporters for not discussing cabinet appointments with parliament.
"Some of the names published have so far caused major concern...they (pro-Khatami factions) are trying to stop the Majlis from doing its legal duty," Resalat newspaper said.
